q1: `<meta charset="UTF-8">` declares the character encoding the browser should use to interpret the page's text.
q2: Without a correct charset declaration, the browser guesses the encoding, and accented characters, curly quotes, or emoji often render as garbled symbols.
q3: The attribute is `initial-scale`, which sets the starting zoom level (usually `1`, meaning 100%).
q4: False — the viewport tag only stops the browser from forcing a zoomed-out desktop-width view. Actual responsiveness still requires responsive CSS.
q5: The viewport tag sets the page width to the device width and sets the initial zoom, and that combination prevents the forced zoomed-out desktop view — but it does not by itself guarantee a responsive layout, which depends on your CSS.
q6: The description meta tag mainly shapes the snippet text search engines show under the page title in results; it is not itself a ranking factor.
q7: A good description is a genuine plain-language summary, and search engines may substitute their own snippet text; it does not directly affect ranking, and it does have visible effects on how results look.
q8: The correct value is `icon`, e.g. `<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico">`.
q9: The head is missing `<meta charset="UTF-8">`, which is the tag responsible for correct text rendering; nothing else in that head affects character rendering.
q10: The conventional order is charset first (so the browser can read the rest of the head correctly), then viewport, then title, then description and other metadata.
